series: Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.1 · October 2026
title: The CPAT Mitigation Module: Methods in Brief

slides.title: The CPAT Mitigation Module: Methods in Brief
slides.subtitle: What a finance ministry's climate model computes, and how to read its results
slides.message: CPAT's mitigation module fits in fourteen equations. A carbon price bites on coal far more than on road fuel, and power-sector results rest on two judgment calls that ministries should know about.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity
slides.notes: The paper states the method of the World Bank-IMF Climate Policy Assessment Tool's mitigation module from the rebuilt and tested version (CPAT-AI).

slides.title: The module is a one-way chain from prices to revenue, with lagged feedback

points.text: supply cost, plus taxes, less subsidies, plus the carbon charge and VAT on it.
income, an efficiency trend and two price margins: how much the stock is used, and how efficient it becomes.
an engineering model, then accounting; revenue moves output a year later.

slides.source: Working paper 5.1, Figure 1; CPAT documentation; CPAT-AI equation list.

slides.title: A $50 carbon price cuts industrial coal use by a third and road fuel by about 6%
slides.note: A charge per tonne of CO₂ is large relative to cheap, carbon-rich coal and small relative to heavily taxed road fuel. Each fuel responds to its own price alone: no switching outside power, cooking and road vehicles.
slides.source: Working paper 5.1, Table 1. Stylized prices; IPCC (2006) emission factors; CPAT default elasticities, low- and middle-income countries.

slides.title: Every price and every response can be traced, and the rebuild made the rules explicit

points.text: A floating tax or subsidy absorbs world-price changes, but a positive tax never falls below its last level, so rises in taxed fuels reach consumers.

points.lead: Non-price policies act on efficiency only.
points.text: Standards and feebates enter as shadow prices that cut fuel use without raising the price paid.
A sudden price jump gets its full long-run response in one year; phased reforms are little affected.
Total GDP drives demand with one elasticity.

slides.source: Working paper 5.1, sections on prices and demand; CPAT-AI equation list (M2.2, A2.1, M3.1); issues I62, I71.

slides.title: Power-sector results rest on two judgment calls

points.lead: A logit shares new investment by cost.
points.text: Its curvature was "set subjectively at 2" and has never been estimated; every permitted technology always gets some share.
Wind and solar can each add about 2 percentage points of the system a year in most countries; under a large carbon price the cap often decides the answer.

points.lead: The cost of capital differs by source.
points.text: The documentation describes 7.5–15% by income group; the model uses a country rate plus a technology premium.

slides.source: CPAT documentation (2023 edition); CPAT-AI methods notes (Power); working paper 5.1, power-sector section.

slides.title: The logit is a penalized cost minimum; a quadratic penalty drops uncompetitive technologies to zero

points.text: acts as an entropy penalty on concentration worth $22.5/MWh here.
the logit gives oil 1.4% at more than 2.5 times the cost of solar; the alternative, nothing.

slides.title: The rebuild found errors that changed results, and fixed them

points.text: Legacy added a policy's one-off effect on output to the growth rate every year (bug L24).

points.lead: Power plants arrived a year late.
points.text: New capacity was sized for this year's demand although it comes online next year (L67).
Their shadow price was computed but not applied (L87).
including a wrong sign on the electricity markup and no equation for the output feedback; a corrected edition was published on 31 October 2026.

slides.title: Read CPAT as a first estimate for phased, medium-term reforms

points.text: a model with no lags, little switching and a fixed world should not guide fiscal decisions.
its biases mostly have known signs, its elasticities are checked against meta-analyses (paper 5.4), and its responses against other models (paper 5.3).
sudden price shocks, coal-to-gas switching in industry, large economies that move world prices, and power paths under high carbon prices.
